notes.short: Dark as Kedar's tents, lovely as Solomon's curtains
notes.about: The verse names two things, then two likenesses, in turn. The tents of Kedar answer to dark, and the curtains of Solomon to lovely.
notes.evidence: Lowth says the last line is to be divided and its parts applied separately to what goes before. Kingsbury, in Barnes' Notes, and Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) read dark as the tents of Kedar and lovely as the curtains of Solomon.

cites.quote: The last line here is also to be divided and separately applied to the preceding

cites.quote: Dark-hued, as the tents of Kedar with their black goats' hair coverings, rough and weather-stained ... but comely (beautiful) as the rich hangings which adorn the pavilion of Solomon.

notes.short: A wall, not a door: the bride stood firm
notes.about: Asked what to do for their young sister, the brothers answer in a picture: a wall they will crown with silver, a door they will board up with cedar. The wall is a maiden firm against every advance, the door one open to them. The bride says she is such a wall, and so has won the king's favor.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.means: a maiden firm in chastity, on whom no advance can be made, who will be honored; the door is one open to seduction, who must be guarded

notes.evidence: T. L. Kingsbury (Barnes' Notes) says the brothers answer in the form of a parable: a wall is a sister steadfast in chastity, a door one open to seduction, and the bride has shown she is such a fortress-wall. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the wall is used as a figure of firmness of character: a maiden closed to seduction is like a wall, one open to it like a door.

cites.quote: The answer is given in the form of a parable: "If she be a wall," i. e., stedfast in chastity and virtue, one on whom no light advances can be made, then let us honor and reward her. ... But "if she be a door," light-minded and accessible to seduction ... She has shown herself to be such a fortress-wall as her brothers have alluded to, and her reward has been the royal favor.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A wall stands firm and withstands every assault if it serves its purpose (which is here presupposed, where it is used as a figure of firmness of character). A door, on the contrary, is moveable ... A maiden inaccessible to seduction is like a wall, and one accessible to it is like a door.

notes.short: Solomon's vineyard, and the bride's own
notes.about: The bride tells of Solomon's vineyard at Baal-hamon, leased to tenants who each bring a thousand shekels for its fruit. She sets beside it her own vineyard, herself: the thousand are Solomon's, and two hundred go to its keepers, her brothers. So she asks the king to reward those who guarded her.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon
figure.means: the bride's own vineyard, herself, now wholly Solomon's, whose keepers, her brothers who guarded her, should be rewarded as his tenants are

notes.evidence: T. L. Kingsbury (Barnes' Notes) says the bride commends her brothers to the king by another parable: her own vineyard, her beauty and virtue guarded by them, now belongs to Solomon, but the keepers should have their due. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says she makes the vineyard at Baal-hamon a parable of her relation to Solomon and to her brothers, the keepers of her innocence.
notes.limit: The note does not make the vineyard at Baal-hamon a made-up one: both writers take it as a real vineyard of Solomon's, which the bride makes a likeness of her own case.

cites.quote: She next turns to the king, and commends her brothers to his favorable regard by means of another parable. ... The bride also has a vineyard of her own Sol 1:6 , her beauty and virtue faithfully guarded by these same brothers in time past. This vineyard now belongs to Solomon. ... let the faithful keepers have their meed as well.

cites.quote: Shulamith also has a vineyard, which she is as free to dispose of as Solomon of his at Baal-hamon. It is the totality of her personal and mental endowments. ... These are her brothers, the true keepers and protectors of her innocence. ... She makes the case of the vineyard in Baal-hamon a parable of her relation to Solomon on the one hand, and of her relation to her brothers on the other.
